system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-12-28 03:41:00 to 2175-01-01 18:46:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with psoriatic arthritis and undifferentiated IBD, on long-term immunosuppression with Humira, azathioprine, and prednisone, was admitted for one week of profuse sweating and three days of severe exhaustion. Despite being afebrile, his immunocompromised status prompted an extensive infectious workup, including blood cultures, serologies, lumbar puncture, and imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, MRI brain), all of which were unremarkable. A right calf lesion was biopsied and found consistent with erythema nodosum, with no evidence of infection. Given the temporal association of symptom onset with his last Humira dose, the medication was discontinued. Azathioprine was held during admission but resumed at discharge, along with prednisone. Trigger point injections were administered for worsening cervical headaches, as Botox was deferred due to diagnostic uncertainty. The patient improved clinically, remained stable, and was discharged home with follow-up arranged in rheumatology and dermatology.
problems: Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis
Secondary diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, not stated as uncontrolled, or unspecified
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

Brief Hospital Course:
This is a ___ year old man with a poorly controlled psoriatic 
arthritis presented with severe left knee pain and swelling due 
to psoriatic arthritis flare. A left knee arthrocentesis was 
performed and revealed a WBC of 58 K with 94% PMNs and no 
crystals, supporting an inflammatory etiology.  Though he had a 
mild leukocytosis, the negative gram stain, negative blood and 
joint culture, continued ability to weight bear/ambulate, and 
lack of fever argued against septic arthritis.  DVT was ruled 
out given negative lower extremity ultrasound.  It was unlikely 
to be gout, or pseudogout given lack of crystals in joint 
aspirate.   He was started empirically on antibiotics 
(Vancomycin and Cipro - did not give ceftriaxone due to Keflex 
allergy), which were discontinued after synovial culture 
returned negative.  He was kept on prednisone, initially at his 
home dose (30 mg daily), and then at a higher dose (60 mg daily) 
when synovial gram stain was negative and preliminary synovial 
cultures showed no growth.  His knee pain and inflammation 
significantly improved for several days, but then he developed 
mild-moderate calf pain, along with continued pain in his other 
joints and muscles, without clinical signs of inflammation such 
as erythema, warmth, or increased edema. He was started on 
Neurontin per his rheumatologist with presumptive diagnosis of 
fibromyalgia, and a repeat leg ultrasound was obtained which 
showed no fluid collections to suggest abscesses or findings of 
DVT, or rupture of ___ cyst. He was observed for additional 
days for his calf pain which he strongly believed that it was 
consistent with erythema nodosum as he had multiple flares (I 
know my body) in the past that responded to NSAID, Prednisone, 
and occasionally potassium iodide. Because he had no concerning 
findings on physical examination (except mild focal erythremia 
in posterior calf) and negative ultrasound, he was discharged 
home. However, he was asked to follow up with his 
Rheumatologist, ID, or PCP if his pain persists or he develops 
new findings such as increased swelling or progressive 
erythremia to consider advanced imaging. Again, he remained 
afebrile without signs or symptoms of infection. In regards to 
his psoriatic arthritis, at time of admission, he was having an 
active flare with swelling and pain in his elbows, wrists, 
knees, ankles, and toes. He was failing treatment with Simponi 
and awaiting insurance approval for Cimzia.  He was continued on 
azathioprine, indomethacin, alendronate, calcium, vitamin D, and 
Bactrim.  His prednisone dose was increased to twice his prior 
dose (60 mg daily). His primary rheumatologist evaluated him and 
agreed with doubling the steroid dose. The patient also had 
cervical headache which usually accompanies his flares. This was 
treated, as previously, with pain consult and bupivacaine 
injection into cervical trigger points.
  
# DMII: Pt has steroid induced diabetes.  He was followed by the 
___ and controlled his own insulin sliding scale during the 
hospital stay, with good glycemic control.  He was able to stick 
to his You Fit diet throughout the hospital stay with assistance 
from nutrition, and was pleased to lose 12 lbs over 1 week on 
the diet.  He was kept on his home dose of aspirin.
.  
# Hypertension: Steroid-induced.  He was continued on his home 
doses of HCTZ, lisinopril, and metoprolol.
.  
# Costochondritis: Pt has recurrent costochondritis, for which 
he is on indomethacin.  He experienced an episode of chest pain 
during the hospital stay consistent with his typical 
costochondritis pain.  EKG was normal, and the pain resolved 
with Dilaudid.
.
# OSA: Patient used CPAP ___ cm at night throughout hospital 
stay.    
.
# Hyperlipidemia: Home dose of pravastatin was continued.

Brief Hospital Course:
This is a ___ year old man with a poorly controlled psoriatic 
arthritis presented with severe left knee pain and swelling due 
to psoriatic arthritis flare. A left knee arthrocentesis was 
performed and revealed a WBC of 58 K with 94% PMNs and no 
crystals, supporting an inflammatory etiology.  Though he had a 
mild leukocytosis, the negative gram stain, negative blood and 
joint culture, continued ability to weight bear/ambulate, and 
lack of fever argued against septic arthritis.  DVT was ruled 
out given negative lower extremity ultrasound.  It was unlikely 
to be gout, or pseudogout given lack of crystals in joint 
aspirate.   He was started empirically on antibiotics 
(Vancomycin and Cipro - did not give ceftriaxone due to Keflex 
allergy), which were discontinued after synovial culture 
returned negative.  He was kept on prednisone, initially at his 
home dose (30 mg daily), and then at a higher dose (60 mg daily) 
when synovial gram stain was negative and preliminary synovial 
cultures showed no growth.  His knee pain and inflammation 
significantly improved for several days, but then he developed 
mild-moderate calf pain, along with continued pain in his other 
joints and muscles, without clinical signs of inflammation such 
as erythema, warmth, or increased edema. He was started on 
Neurontin per his rheumatologist with presumptive diagnosis of 
fibromyalgia, and a repeat leg ultrasound was obtained which 
showed no fluid collections to suggest abscesses or findings of 
DVT, or rupture of ___ cyst. He was observed for additional 
days for his calf pain which he strongly believed that it was 
consistent with erythema nodosum as he had multiple flares (I 
know my body) in the past that responded to NSAID, Prednisone, 
and occasionally potassium iodide. Because he had no concerning 
findings on physical examination (except mild focal erythremia 
in posterior calf) and negative ultrasound, he was discharged 
home. However, he was asked to follow up with his 
Rheumatologist, ID, or PCP if his pain persists or he develops 
new findings such as increased swelling or progressive 
erythremia to consider advanced imaging. Again, he remained 
afebrile without signs or symptoms of infection. In regards to 
his psoriatic arthritis, at time of admission, he was having an 
active flare with swelling and pain in his elbows, wrists, 
knees, ankles, and toes. He was failing treatment with Simponi 
and awaiting insurance approval for Cimzia.  He was continued on 
azathioprine, indomethacin, alendronate, calcium, vitamin D, and 
Bactrim.  His prednisone dose was increased to twice his prior 
dose (60 mg daily). His primary rheumatologist evaluated him and 
agreed with doubling the steroid dose. The patient also had 
cervical headache which usually accompanies his flares. This was 
treated, as previously, with pain consult and bupivacaine 
injection into cervical trigger points.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with severe pain in your left leg and knee. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. It started yesterday evening—pins and needles in my left heel, then sharp pain shooting up my calf. Within an hour, it reached my knee. I took morphine at home, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you have a history of psoriatic arthritis, correct? Has it been flaring recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bad—swelling in my wrists, knees, toes. I got a steroid shot last week, and things were improving. But this leg pain came back out of nowhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. In the ER, your X-ray showed no fracture, and the ultrasound ruled out a blood clot. We’re going to keep you for pain control and further evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it might be an infection or something serious. I’ve had joint issues before, but this feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. We’re going to check the fluid in your knee to make sure it’s not septic. We’ll do a procedure called arthrocentesis—drawing fluid out with a needle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’ve had that done before. But I’m also stressed—I’m in the middle of a weight-loss and insulin program called 'You Turn.' I was supposed to restart tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll make sure you stay on your insulin and diet. Nutrition is already involved, and you can continue your sliding scale. We’ll help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished the arthrocentesis. We removed fluid from your left knee. It looked cloudy, which suggests inflammation, not infection—but we’ll send it to the lab to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected? But why so much pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain is likely from a flare of your psoriatic arthritis. The fluid had a high white blood cell count—58,000—mostly neutrophils. That’s inflammatory, not septic. But we’ll start antibiotics just in case until we get the culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to Keflex—be careful with the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’re using vancomycin and ciprofloxacin—safe for you. We’ll stop them once we confirm no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your joint fluid culture came back negative—no bacteria grew. Blood cultures are also negative so far. We’re stopping the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s just a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re increasing your prednisone from 30mg to 60mg daily to help calm the inflammation. Your rheumatologist agrees with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being on high-dose steroids, but I know they help. My blood sugar’s been harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. You’re doing well with your insulin sliding scale. Your sugars have been in the 100–140 range—excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve also been sticking to the You Fit diet. I lost 3 pounds already this week!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fantastic. We’ll keep nutrition involved to support you. Now, about your pain—your knee is improving, but you mentioned new calf pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a dull ache now, not sharp. But I know my body—I’ve had erythema nodosum before. This feels like the start of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked—an ultrasound of your calf showed no DVT, no abscess, no ruptured Baker’s cyst. There’s mild redness, but no significant swelling or warmth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it still be erythema nodosum? It usually responds to steroids or potassium iodide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But without clear nodules or systemic symptoms, we’re not certain. We’ll keep monitoring. For now, we’re adding gabapentin—your rheumatologist thinks it might help with nerve-type pain or fibromyalgia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your CRP and ESR are elevated—66 and 60—so there’s still inflammation, but your knee is much better. How’s the calf?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still tender. I’m glad the antibiotics are stopped. I was worried about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. Your cultures remained negative. No sign of infection. We’re continuing the high-dose prednisone for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other joints? My neck’s been killing me again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your cervical headaches often flare with joint pain. We’ve scheduled a trigger point injection with pain management today—same as last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. That usually helps. And my chest pain last night—was that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had substernal pain, but EKG was normal, and it responded to dilaudid. Likely costochondritis—your usual pattern. We’ll keep you on indomethacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished the trigger point injection in your neck. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already a bit better. The tightness is easing. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your calf ultrasound today was unchanged—no new fluid or clot. We think the pain is part of your inflammatory flare, not a separate issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not going home with antibiotics or new tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. You’re afebrile, no signs of infection, and improving. We’ll discharge you tomorrow if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my meds? I want to make sure I’m set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re tapering your prednisone to 20mg daily. You’ll continue azathioprine, indomethacin, and now gabapentin three times a day. Your insulin doses are unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the morphine? I still have breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home with sustained-release morphine twice daily and hydromorphone for breakthrough pain—five days' supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And compression socks? My legs swell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home with a pair. Wear them during the day, especially if you’re sitting or standing for long periods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made great progress. Your knee is much less swollen, and you’re walking better. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m ready to get back to my program. But what if the calf pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on it. If the pain worsens, or you see increasing redness or swelling, call your rheumatologist, ID, or PCP. They may consider more imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up? With rheumatology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have an appointment in one week. They’re also working on getting approval for Cimzia, since Simponi isn’t controlling your disease well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already. I’ll keep up with my diet and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done an excellent job managing your health. Keep it up. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be out by noon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with severe psoriatic arthritis and multiple comorbidities was admitted for acute left leg and knee pain. He presented with a flare of his arthritis, including swelling and severe pain in the left knee, with radiating symptoms to the calf. Imaging ruled out fracture and DVT, and arthrocentesis revealed inflammatory fluid with no crystals or infection. Empiric antibiotics were started but discontinued after cultures remained negative. Prednisone was increased to 60 mg daily, resulting in significant improvement. He developed mild calf pain, which was monitored and attributed to inflammatory or neuropathic causes; gabapentin was initiated. A cervical trigger point injection was performed for headache, and he maintained good glycemic control on his insulin regimen. He was discharged home with a prednisone taper, continued immunosuppression, and follow-up arranged with rheumatology.
